title: The Day of Vengeance on Edom and the Nations
summary: The nations are summoned to hear that the LORD is angry with them all and has devoted their armies to destruction, while the very heavens roll up like a scroll. His sword falls especially on Edom, which becomes a sacrifice, a land of burning pitch, and a haunt of owls, jackals, and wild creatures forever. Readers are invited to search the scroll of the LORD and see that his word will not fail.
story: Chapters 34 and 35 form a pair that closes the poetry of the book's first half before the narratives of chapters 36 to 39. They set side by side two destinies: a land turned to wilderness (chapter 34) and a wilderness turned into a garden (chapter 35). Chapter 34 gathers up the judgments on the nations from chapters 13 to 23 and 24 to 27, now focused on Edom as the representative enemy of God's people. The reversal it describes, a land returned to chaos, prepares by contrast for the highway of joy in chapter 35 and for the comfort announced in chapter 40.
historical:
Edom lay south and southeast of the Dead Sea, in the rugged highlands east of the Arabah valley. Its people were traced back to Esau, Jacob's brother (Genesis 36), and the two nations had a long history of hostility, from Edom's refusal to let Israel pass through its land (Numbers 20:14-21) to its wars with the kings of Judah. Edom was remembered with special bitterness because it gloated over and took part in the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC (Obadiah 10-14; Psalm 137:7). Bozrah (verse 6), identified with modern Buseirah in southern Jordan, was one of its chief cities. Edom declined in the following centuries; by the later Persian period Arab peoples, and afterward the Nabataeans, controlled its homeland, and many Edomites had moved into southern Judah, which came to be called Idumea.

When chapters 34 and 35 were written is debated. The traditional view assigns them to Isaiah in the eighth century BC as prophecy. Many critical scholars date them to the exile or later, because Edom's betrayal in 587 or 586 BC seems to lie behind them and because their style and themes, especially in chapter 35, are very close to chapters 40 to 66. Some even speak of these chapters as a bridge written to join the two halves of the book. Others hold that Isaiah's own words were later adapted in this setting. On any view, Edom here stands for more than one small nation: it represents every power that sets itself against God and his people.
cultural:
Verses 2 and 5 use the language of herem, the practice of devoting something wholly to God, usually by destruction, so that no one could profit from it. It was known among Israel's neighbors as well; the Moabite king Mesha, in his ninth-century inscription, boasts of devoting an Israelite town to his god. Verse 6 pictures the judgment as a sacrifice, with the fat and blood of animals that belonged to God in Israel's own offerings (Leviticus 3:16-17).

The imagery of verses 9 to 15 describes a land made uninhabitable. Streams become tar and soil becomes sulfur, recalling Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24), which lay in the same region. Owls, ravens, jackals, ostriches, hyenas, and wild goats are creatures of ruins and wilderness, and their presence meant human life had ended. The "night creature" of verse 14 translates the Hebrew lilit, which is related to Mesopotamian names for female demons of the night; later Jewish legend built stories of a demon called Lilith around the word. Many translators take it here as a night bird or other animal, and the verse is best read as part of a picture of desolation rather than a lesson in demonology. The "measuring line" and "plumb line" of verse 11 were builder's tools, used here in reverse to lay out a ruin.
literary: The chapter moves from the universal (verses 1 to 4) to the particular (verses 5 to 17), a pattern common in the prophets. It opens with a summons like a courtroom call, bidding the nations and the earth to listen. The cosmic images of verse 4 describe God's judgment as shaking the heavens themselves. Verse 11 deliberately echoes Genesis 1:2, using the words tohu and bohu (formless and void), so that Edom's judgment is pictured as creation undone. The chapter ends not with silence but with the assurance of God's word: readers are told to search "the scroll of the LORD" and find that every creature he named will be in its place, because his mouth has ordered it. The desolation itself is a fulfilled word.

outline.t: The nations summoned and the heavens rolled up
The LORD's sword and the sacrifice in Bozrah
The day of vengeance: Edom a burning waste
Chaos and wild creatures take possession
Search the scroll of the LORD: his word will not fail

doctrines.note: God's judgment on the nations is described as a day of vengeance and a year of recompense "for the cause of Zion" (verse 8). He defends his people and holds their oppressors to account.
Verse 16 appeals to a written word from the LORD that will be fulfilled in every detail. God's spoken word is reliable because he himself has ordered it.
The use of formless and void (verse 11) shows judgment as the reversal of creation. The God who brings order out of chaos can also withdraw it from a people who oppose him.

words.note: Charam, to devote to destruction. The verb describes putting something under the ban, wholly given over to God and removed from human use, usually by destruction. It is used of the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 6:21) and here of the nations and Edom. It is among the Bible's hardest words, and it frames the judgment as God's act, not human vengeance.

Naqam, vengeance. In the Old Testament vengeance belongs to God (Deuteronomy 32:35), and it means the restoration of justice by a rightful authority, not personal spite. Verse 8 pairs it with recompense, repayment that settles accounts on behalf of Zion.

Tohu, formlessness or chaos. The word appears in Genesis 1:2 for the earth before God ordered it, and in verse 11 for the line stretched over Edom. Its use here presents judgment as a return to the state before creation.

christ: The New Testament borrows the cosmic images of verse 4 for the coming of the Son of Man and the end of the age. Jesus spoke of the stars falling from the sky and the powers of the heavens being shaken (Matthew 24:29), and Revelation describes the sky receding like a scroll being rolled up (Revelation 6:14). The smoke that rises forever (verse 10) also reappears in Revelation's judgment on Babylon (Revelation 19:3). The link to Christ is that the New Testament places final judgment in his hands. The phrase "a day of vengeance" returns in Isaiah 61:2, and when Jesus read that passage in the synagogue at Nazareth, he stopped before the words about vengeance (Luke 4:18-19), announcing the year of the Lord's favor first.

hard.q: How should a reader understand a chapter that pictures God's sword bathed in blood and a whole nation devoted to destruction?
hard.a:
The chapter is poetry of judgment, full of deliberate exaggeration and stock images drawn from ancient war and sacrifice, and it is not a description of a single battle. Its first readers heard it as the vindication of victims: Edom had helped destroy Jerusalem, and the chapter assures the powerless that God will not ignore injustice. The language of sacrifice presents judgment as belonging to God alone, not as permission for human vengeance, and elsewhere Scripture forbids God's people to take revenge themselves (Leviticus 19:18; Romans 12:19).

Readers still differ on how to hold these texts. Some stress that Edom here is a symbol of every power opposed to God, so that the chapter is about the final defeat of evil. Others stress the historical Edom and note that the region did become desolate and its people absorbed into others. Many Christians also read such chapters in light of the cross, where God's judgment on sin is borne by God himself in Christ, which does not remove judgment but shows it is never God's delight.

questions: Edom was judged in part for gloating over Jerusalem's fall. Why does Scripture treat rejoicing at another's disaster so seriously?
The chapter pictures judgment as creation unraveling. How does sin undo the good order God made, in a life or a society?
Verse 16 invites readers to check the scroll of the LORD and see that his word does not fail. What difference does it make to trust God's word when the world seems out of control?
